messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 79
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus Webb's Story

Marcus Webb was seventy-nine years old when he finally walked into the mental health clinic on a Tuesday morning, his weathered hands trembling slightly as he signed the intake form. He had worked in warehouse logistics for fifty-three years—a man of routine, of pallets and inventory systems, of the kind of order that made sense. But for the past decade, that order had been crumbling, and Marcus knew it. He had come because his daughter, whom he had not spoken to in three years, had sent him a letter saying she was worried he would not live much longer if things continued as they were.

The memories that haunted Marcus did not come to him as a coherent story. They came in fragments, each one arriving with the full force of terror even though he could rarely see them clearly. He was eight years old again, standing in the pine woods behind his family's house in rural North Carolina, but the image would not hold—what remained vivid was the feeling, a suffocating dread that bloomed in his chest without warning. Other pieces surfaced without order: the sound of his mother's voice, thin and pleading; the smell of whiskey, sharp and acrid; a door slamming so hard the whole house seemed to shake. When he tried deliberately to piece these moments together into something that made sense, they scattered like startled birds. The harder he concentrated, the more elusive they became. What he knew with absolute certainty, what his body knew without question, was that something terrible had happened between his parents in those woods, that he had witnessed it, and that the world had never felt safe in the same way afterward.

The triggers had always been there, but they had intensified as Marcus aged and the warehouse job began to feel less like shelter and more like exposure. The smell of alcohol—whether from a coworker's breath or a spill in the break room—sent him into a state of hypervigilance that could last for hours. Doors slamming, a common occurrence in the warehouse environment where loading bays opened and closed throughout the day, made his heart race and his palms sweat. Worst of all was when the warehouse received shipments from a supplier in the mountains, and Marcus found himself helping to organize outdoor storage in a wooded area behind the facility. The smell of pine trees, the sound of wind through branches, the particular quality of light filtering through leaves—these sent him spiraling into a panic he could not name or control.

By his mid-seventies, Marcus had developed an intricate system of avoidance that had begun to consume his life. He drank heavily most evenings, a habit that had started as a way to quiet the fragmented memories and had become a daily necessity. He picked fights with coworkers over trivial matters—a misplaced inventory sheet, a perceived slight—just to feel something other than the dread that lived beneath his skin. He surrounded himself constantly with people: he went to bars even when he did not want to drink, he joined a senior center even though he felt no genuine connection to anyone there, he called acquaintances at odd hours just to hear another voice in his apartment. Alone, even for an hour, the memories would surface in pieces, and the emotion would come without the image, a kind of free-floating terror that had nowhere to attach itself and therefore attached itself to everything.

His daughter had stopped calling after he had shown up drunk to his grandson's high school graduation. His supervisor had begun documenting his absences and his mood swings. The warehouse had become a place where Marcus felt increasingly unstable, where the triggers were everywhere and his coping strategies were failing him more visibly each month.

What frightened Marcus most was the possibility that at seventy-nine, it was too late to make sense of what had happened to him, too late to stop running. But what had finally brought him to the clinic was simpler: the realization that he was running himself to death, and that his daughter might be right.
